name: LuaJIT
summary: An embeddable Lua 5.1-compatible runtime that combines an assembler interpreter with a trace-based JIT compiler, exposes JIT and trace controls, and integrates a C declaration and data interface through FFI.

features.name: Interpreter plus trace-based JIT
features.description: LuaJIT's official project description identifies a high-speed assembler interpreter and a trace compiler with SSA-based optimizations and tuned code-generation backends. The JIT library documents automatic compilation, trace flushing, and per-function enablement controls.
benefits: Retains an interpreter path while specializing hot execution traces
Allows generated code to use runtime observations for dynamic-language performance
costs: Trace formation, exits, invalidation, and generated-code caching add runtime complexity
Performance depends on workload shape and the compiler's ability to form useful traces

features.name: Integrated C FFI boundary
features.description: LuaJIT's official FFI documentation allows Lua code to parse C declarations, call external C functions, and create or access C data structures. It states that the FFI is integrated into LuaJIT and that C calls can be inlined in JIT-compiled code.
benefits: Reduces the amount of handwritten binding code for C libraries
Provides low-level C-compatible data access from Lua code
costs: C ABI, layout, and lifetime assumptions become part of Lua code's correctness surface
Native calls and mutable C data reduce the isolation of the managed language boundary

features.name: Embeddable Lua runtime
features.description: LuaJIT describes Lua as embeddable or standalone and documents compatibility with the Lua 5.1 API and ABI. The fixed source is organized as a runtime implementation with public Lua and JIT interfaces.
benefits: Supports use as scripting middleware inside host applications
Preserves a familiar Lua-facing API while adding JIT and FFI facilities
costs: Hosts must manage runtime lifecycle and native integration boundaries
Compatibility and extension facilities increase the surface that embedders must understand

mathematical_views.question: Under what runtime observations can LuaJIT transition from interpreted execution to a compiled trace and later return through exits or flushes?
assumptions: Interpreter states, trace roots, side traces, and generated-code cache entries are abstract states
Trace compilation and cache flushing are transitions controlled by runtime observations and JIT settings
The view abstracts processor-specific code generation and exact hot-loop thresholds

mathematical_views.question: How do parsed C declarations, Lua-visible C data, native calls, and JIT-generated accesses compose at the FFI boundary?
assumptions: C declarations and data objects are typed interface vertices connected to Lua values and native symbols
A call or field access is valid only when the declared ABI and layout contract is satisfied
The model abstracts platform ABI details and does not prove safety of arbitrary native declarations

mathematical_views.question: Which combinations of stable runtime behavior and FFI access patterns are suitable for trace specialization without changing observable Lua semantics?
assumptions: Observed execution paths provide candidate guards and specialization inputs
Trace exits preserve a fallback path when observations no longer hold
This is a hypothesis about an analysis lens, not a claim that every trace or FFI operation is optimized

benefits: Adaptive specialization while retaining an interpreter fallback
costs: Trace lifecycle, exits, and code-cache management increase runtime complexity

benefits: Low-boilerplate access to C functions and layouts
costs: Native ABI and memory assumptions enter the dynamic-language program
Host lifecycle and compatibility responsibilities remain
